entries.center: Genesis 4:1–5 and 4:25–26; the names YHWH (the personal name, printed 'LORD'), Elohim ('God'), and the compound YHWH Elohim ('LORD God', Gen 2:4b–3:24); 'Son of Man' (Dan 7:13; Mark 14:62; Acts 7:56); Seth, Enosh, Noah (Gen 4:25–5; 6:9).

claims.layer_a: Gen 4:1 — 'The man knew (yada') Eve his wife; she conceived and bore Cain,' Eve: qaniti ish et-YHWH — the particle 'et is of uncertain force (JPS/Sefaria note); every major translation resolves it 'with the help of the LORD' (ESV/NIV/NASB) or 'from the LORD' (KJV/NKJV). A minority grammatical reading takes 'et as the direct-object marker — 'I have gotten a man — YHWH' (Ellicott, who read Eve as expecting the Gen 3:15 deliverer); even on that reading Adam remains the subject who 'knew' Eve and she 'conceived.' 4:2 — 'she again bore (wattoseph laledet) his brother Abel,' no second 'knew/conceived' stated. Control: 4:25 — 'Adam knew his wife again… another seed in place of Abel.'
claims.layer_b: Mainstream commentaries (Keil & Delitzsch; Cambridge) read Eve's words as thanksgiving linked to the Gen 3:15 hope; the non-repetition in 4:2 is ordinary Hebrew narrative economy. A different-paternity speculation exists outside Genesis and outside the mainstream — Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, the Zohar, the Gnostic Gospel of Philip — concerning Cain's paternity; its modern 'serpent seed' form is a 19th/20th-century construction.
claims.layer_c: The step from 'not repeated' to 'different conception/father' is an argument from silence — it adds a partner or mechanism the text never names, against the text calling Abel Cain's 'brother' and Seth his replacement seed through a renewed 'Adam knew his wife.'
claims.text: Cain and Abel were conceived differently — Gen 4:1 states 'Adam knew Eve' for Cain; 4:2 does not repeat it for Abel.

claims.layer_a: 4:3 — Cain's offering is explicitly 'to YHWH' (la-YHWH); 4:4 — Abel 'also brought' (hevi gam-hu), no new recipient named; 4:4–5 — the same YHWH has regard for one offering and not the other; Genesis states no reason for the difference.
claims.layer_b: The canon supplies its own reasons, neither about recipients: faith (Heb 11:4 — 'by faith Abel offered a more acceptable sacrifice') and deeds (1 John 3:12 — Cain 'of the evil one,' explained in the verse by evil deeds vs righteous ones). Henry/Keil: regard for the offerer before the offering; Abel's 'firstborn… fat' (first and best) vs Cain's unqualified 'fruit.' Produce offerings are legitimate (Lev 2), so a blood-only explanation is a contested minority view. Recorded disagreement: Genesis itself states no reason, and scholars continue to disagree about the reason beyond the faith/deeds answers — this entry does not settle it (see open questions).
claims.layer_c: The split of recipients is imported; the passage names one recipient, one 'also,' one judge of both.
claims.text: Cain's offering went to 'the LORD' and Abel's to 'God' — different recipients.

claims.layer_a: Gen 1 uses Elohim alone; Gen 2:4b–3:24 narrates with the compound 'YHWH Elohim' as one subject with singular verbs (the serpent dialogue excepted); Gen 4 uses YHWH alone. Exod 6:2 — Elohim speaks: 'I am YHWH.'
claims.layer_b: No historic mainstream reading splits the names into actors. The separate-actor systems that did exist are different schemes: Marcion (OT God vs the Father of Jesus), Gnostic systems (an ignorant demiurge fashioning the whole world), Segal's 'two powers' (God + a mediator figure — documented as a rabbinic heresy label, rejected). Source criticism reads the name variation as human source traditions about one God, 'YHWH Elohim' as a redactional bridge asserting identity (the classic JEDP scheme has been substantially revised in modern scholarship, and scholars disagree about the sources — the unity point holds across those disagreements); the traditional reading maps the names to aspects (Elohim/justice, YHWH/mercy) of the same God.
claims.layer_c: The teaching conflates three historically distinct schemes (Marcion's split, Gnostic dualism, J/E authorship) into a fourth none of them holds, and must set aside the compound subject of Gen 2–3 and Exod 6:2's self-identification.
claims.text: 'LORD,' 'God,' and 'LORD God' name separate actors in Genesis.
claims.verdict_note: As a claim about what Genesis presents: the compound subject 'YHWH Elohim' acting with singular verbs, and Elohim's 'I am YHWH' (Exod 6:2), run against two actors; the separate-actor schemes in Layer B are different schemes — none of them holds this claim, so no tradition exists to make it a contested reading.

claims.layer_a: Dan 7:13 — 'one like a son of man' comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days; Daniel's own interpretation gives the kingdom to 'the holy ones of the Most High' (7:18, 22, 27). The definite title occurs ~81–82 times in the NT, overwhelmingly Jesus' self-designation; Acts 7:56 (Stephen) is the only direct application to Jesus by another speaker outside the Gospels.
claims.layer_b: Mainstream Daniel scholarship (Collins) reads the human-like figure as symbolising the holy ones of the Most High; individual/messianic readings are a defended minority, developed in the Similitudes of 1 Enoch (whose dating is debated). Historic Christian interpretation identifies Jesus as Daniel's figure; Stephen's 'standing' is glossed (welcome/advocacy) but unexplained in the text.
claims.layer_c: No text connects the title to Cain/Abel or to a YHWH/Elohim distinction; the connection is supplied whole by the teaching.
claims.text: The 'Son of Man' title is explained by Christ fulfilling the Cain/Abel pattern.
claims.verdict_note: The title is DOCUMENTED as attested; its explanation by the Cain/Abel pattern is the teaching's own inference.

claims.layer_a: Greek Ioudas is the Greek form of Hebrew Yehudah ('praised'); English 'Jude' and 'Judas' render the same Greek name.
claims.layer_b: The name was very common — the NT names several men Judas/Jude; historic interpretation draws no guilt by association from the name itself.
claims.layer_c: No inference added — the detail stands as stated.
claims.text: Judas is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yehudah (Judah).

claims.layer_a: Gen 37:26–27 — Judah proposes selling Joseph ('what profit… he is our brother, our own flesh'); the brothers agree, and Joseph is sold for 20 shekels (37:28). Reuben had proposed the pit intending rescue (37:21–22).
claims.layer_b: Judah instigated the sale, not the brothers' original murder plot; he later offers himself in Benjamin's place (Gen 44:33).
claims.layer_c: No inference added — the detail stands as stated.
claims.text: Judah played the instigating part in Joseph's betrayal (Gen 37).
claims.verdict_note: With the Layer B nuance: the sale, not the murder plot.

claims.layer_a: John 20:14–15 — Mary sees Jesus, does not recognise him, and, 'supposing him to be the gardener,' asks where the body has been laid; she recognises him when he speaks her name (20:16).
claims.layer_b: Any 'Jesus is the gardener' symbolism is interpretation added to what the text states as a mistaken supposition.
claims.layer_c: The detail is verbatim; only the gardener symbolism layered on it (Layer B) goes past the text.
claims.text: Mary supposed the risen Jesus to be the gardener (John 20:15).

claims.layer_a: John 21:15–17 — a threefold exchange with Peter: 'Feed my lambs' / 'Tend my sheep' / 'Feed my sheep,' each after 'do you love me?'
claims.layer_b: The widespread reading — Peter's restoration after his threefold denial — is historic interpretation; the passage does not state that motive.
claims.layer_c: The words are exact; the restoration motive is interpretation (Layer B), not a statement of the passage.
claims.text: Jesus told Peter to feed/tend his sheep (John 21).
claims.verdict_note: The threefold words; the restoration motive sits in Layer B as interpretation.

claims.layer_a: Gen 4:26 — 'To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD (YHWH)' — as all major translations render it.
claims.layer_b: A minority rabbinic reading exists: Onkelos/Rashi take huchal as a profaning beginning (the start of idolatry); the LXX makes Enosh himself the subject ('he hoped to call on the name').
claims.layer_c: No inference in the detail as major translations render it; the minority reading is recorded in Layer B, adopted by neither the text nor this entry.
claims.text: Seth's son Enosh marks when people began to call on the name of the LORD (Gen 4:26).
claims.verdict_note: As major translations render it; the minority reading rides in Layer B.

claims.layer_a: Gen 6:9 — Noah was 'righteous, blameless (tamim — KJV 'perfect') in his generations; Noah walked with God' — the deity named is Elohim, as with Enoch (Gen 5:24).
claims.layer_b: Tamim means whole/blameless, not sinless perfection (cf. Noah's drunkenness, Gen 9:21).
claims.layer_c: No inference added — the detail stands as stated.
claims.text: Noah was 'perfect in his generations' and walked with God (Gen 6:9).

claims.layer_a: Acts 1:3 — Jesus 'presented himself alive… appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God,' before the Ascension (1:9–11).
claims.layer_b: Acts is the only NT book that gives the forty-day figure; the research records no competing tradition.
claims.layer_c: No inference added — the detail stands as stated.
claims.text: Jesus appeared to his disciples during forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3).

claims.layer_a: Rom 10:9 — 'confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord (Kyrios) and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead'; v.13 then quotes Joel — 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord' — a YHWH text in Joel, applied by Paul to Jesus.
claims.layer_b: Kyrios is the Septuagint's standard substitute for YHWH; Paul's application of Joel's YHWH text (v.13) to calling on Jesus is the context mainstream treatments note.
claims.layer_c: No inference added — the detail stands as stated.
claims.text: Rom 10:9 gives the confession pattern the teaching quotes.

claims.layer_a: The two verses are as recorded under C9 and C12; nothing in either verse, nor in the Seth genealogy of Gen 5, states that the line as a whole knew a way of salvation.
claims.layer_b: The report's caution stands as the mainstream position: Gen 4:26 'does not by itself characterise Seth's line as righteous throughout,' and the Gen 5 genealogy records names and years, not confessions; no historic mainstream reading draws a line-wide knowledge of salvation from these verses.
claims.layer_c: The joining step is the teaching's: two documented verses are fused into a claim about what a whole bloodline 'knew' — a conclusion neither verse states and the genealogy nowhere records.
claims.text: (The teaching's composite conclusion.) Seth's line already knew the way of salvation, as Abel knew how to sacrifice before the law — the C9/C12 verses, joined, are presented as a line-wide, generations-long knowledge.
claims.verdict_note: The two verses are documented; the line-wide conclusion drawn from them is the teaching's joining inference.

claims.layer_a: Gen 25:24 — 'twins in her womb,' one conception; 25:23 — 'the older shall serve the younger,' announced before birth; 25:27 — Esau 'a man of the field (ish sadeh),' Jacob ish tam, 'dwelling in tents' (shepherding explicit only in Haran, Gen 30:31; 31:38–41); 27:41 — Esau's intent to kill; 33:4 — Esau embraces Jacob; they bury Isaac together (35:29). Rom 9:10–13 — Paul stresses 'conceived by one man,' the choice announced before any deeds, 'not by works but by him who calls,' quoting Gen 25:23 and Mal 1:2–3.
claims.layer_b: The elder/younger reversal is a recognised five-case Genesis pattern (Abel; Isaac; Jacob; Joseph — with rulership to Judah, 1 Chr 5:1–2; Ephraim). On Rom 9, scholars divide over individuals (Moo) vs nations/covenant roles (Witherington); 'hated' is often read as the comparative-preference idiom (Gen 29:30–31; Luke 14:26). Both sides agree Paul cites the twins to exclude parentage/works explanations.
claims.layer_c: The parallel holds for the reversal, the shared word 'field,' anger, and a formed intent to kill. The teaching-shape breaks at: one conception (twins) — the very point Paul presses; Jacob not introduced as shepherd, Esau a hunter not a tiller; the exile reversed (the chosen brother flees); no murder — an embrace instead; the chosen brother is the deceiver of Gen 27; and (6) the rejected elder's outcome differs — Esau receives Seir, descendants and kings (Gen 36) and a subordinate blessing from Isaac (27:39–40), where Cain is cursed and his line disappears from the genealogy after Lamech.
claims.text: (Donnie's follow-up question.) The same pattern works for Jacob and Esau.
claims.verdict_note: The reversal pattern is documented and Paul uses it; the conception and shepherd/tiller mechanism does not transfer.

entries.entry_verdict_line: The small details check out almost perfectly; the load-bearing claims — different conceptions, different gods — are the ones the texts do not carry.
open_questions: The teaching's video (URL/transcript/timestamps) was never supplied, so claims were checked as summarised, not against its exact wording.
Which English translation the teaching used for Gen 4:1 is unspecified (both major renderings are recorded in Layer A).
The reason for Cain's rejection beyond the faith/deeds answers — unresolved in the research.
The individual-vs-national scope of Rom 9 — scholars disagree, not resolved.
The collective-vs-individual figure in Dan 7 — not resolved.
The dating of the Similitudes of Enoch — debated, not resolved.
The current form of source criticism after JEDP — scholars disagree, not resolved.
This entry settles none of the above.

teaching_notes.a: Safe as fact: the eight details (C5–C12) as stated; the elder/younger reversal as a Genesis pattern, with Rom 9's own framing ('not by works'); Dan 7 and Acts 7:56 as the title's anchors.
teaching_notes.b: As 'some claim' (Donnie's own preparation only; never part of the teaching layer's read): differing conceptions, split offering-recipients, LORD-vs-God as two actors, the Son of Man / Cain-Abel connection — always attributed, always with the Layer A wording beside them.
teaching_notes.c: The lesson the true history carries: the canon answers its own question — Genesis leaves the reason for Abel's acceptance unstated, and Hebrews and 1 John answer it with faith and deeds; a pattern that needs the text to be silent is a pattern the text hasn't given.

entries.title: The teaching that Cain and Abel were conceived differently, that their offerings went to different gods ('the LORD' vs 'God'), that Christ's 'Son of Man' title fulfils the Cain/Abel pattern, and that Seth's line already knew the way of salvation — checked against the texts.

entries.center: The three English sayings; the claimed long forms ('the blood of the covenant is thicker than the water of the womb'; '…but satisfaction brought it back'; '…though oftentimes better than a master of one'); the word etymology itself — a saying's history is its attestations, in order.

claims.layer_a: Short form: German analogue c.1180 (Reinhart Fuchs, 'kin-blood is not spoiled by water' — identification as the same proverb disputed, see open questions); English, similar sense, Lydgate 1412; modern form in print 1652 (Jenkyn's sermon, delivered 1652, 2nd ed. 1653 — 'Blood is thicker (we say) then water'); older summaries cite Ray's proverb collection (1670), while Phrase Finder's first English print example is Ramsay's Scots collection (1737); popularised by Scott, 1815. Claimed long form: earliest attestation anywhere is 1 Oct 1994 (R. Richard Pustelniak, The Blood Covenant) — stated there as the original, citing no source; spread in the 2000s by Albert Jack's popular-etymology books, also unsourced.
claims.layer_b: Phrase Finder (Gary Martin): the reversal 'has no historical basis and is not biblical,' popularised in the 1990s–2000s by Jack and Pustelniak, neither citing a source. The nearest old comparator — Trumbull, The Blood Covenant (1893), reporting an Arab idea of blood-covenant brothers closer than milk-brothers ('thicker than milk') — is not the claimed wording and does not claim to explain the English proverb; modern retellings appear to have conflated it with the 1994 coinage.
claims.layer_c: The step added: an unsourced 1994 theological coinage presented as a centuries-old original, and the documented meaning (family first, in every century of the record) re-described as the 'reversal.'
claims.text: 'The blood of the covenant is thicker than the water of the womb' is the original of 'blood is thicker than water.'

claims.layer_a: The line begins as 'care killed the cat': Jonson 1598, Shakespeare c.1599; the 'care' form still dictionary-current in 1898 (Brewer). 'Curiosity' form: Irish newspaper 1868; proverb book 1873 (Mair) — Phrase Finder's earliest precise form is later still (Galveston, 1898). The rejoinder: precursor without 'satisfaction,' Galveston 1905; with 'satisfaction,' Waxahachie Daily Light 1909 (Wikipedia listing) / Titusville Herald 1912 (Phrase Finder's first find); standard by 1917–1924 ('As the saying goes…').
claims.layer_b: Reference works treat the rejoinder as a genuine, standard American rejoinder of the early 1900s — an added comeback to a warning, roughly 300 years younger than 'care killed the cat' and decades younger than the curiosity form; no source treats the two-line version as the original.
claims.layer_c: The step added: a true, old rejoinder re-dated into an 'original' — the saying's first three centuries quietly removed.
claims.text: 'Curiosity killed the cat, but satisfaction brought it back' is the original, later cut in half.
claims.verdict_note: The rejoinder is DOCUMENTED, 1905/1909/1912 and standard since; its status as the original is a modern invention.

claims.layer_a: 'Jack of all trades' first in print 1618 (Mynshul, a prison tract; Latin analogue Johannes factotum, Greene 1592). 'Master of none' accreted in stages across the 1700s (variants 1721 / 1732 / 1770; exact wording 1785, Lucas). The 'better than a master of one' tail: no pre-internet attestation in any source searched; traced circulating online by at least 2005, on Wikipedia by 2006 as though it were the 'full saying.'
claims.layer_b: Wikipedia, Idioms Online, Omniglot concur: the tail is a recent addition ('a viral internet myth' — Idioms Online). Even the short form's early tone is contested (Phrase Finder tradition: complimentary early; current scholarship notes most early uses carry criticism) — recorded here as contested, not smoothed over.
claims.layer_c: The step added: a 2000s internet tail presented as the lost ending — and the 1700s accretion of 'master of none' itself skipped, so a three-stage, 400-year growth reads as one ancient sentence.
claims.text: 'Jack of all trades, master of none, though oftentimes better than a master of one' is the original, later cut down.

claims.layer_a: No Hebrew wording, Tanakh/Talmud citation, or proverb-dictionary entry for the blood saying exists in any source consulted; its documented record runs through German, Scots, and English print.
claims.layer_b: The 'Hebrew' framing for blood appears to grow from Pustelniak's theological discussion of Hebrew covenant vocabulary — which presents no Hebrew proverb, wording, or citation.
claims.layer_c: The step added: 'Hebrew' as an authority marker with no Hebrew evidence behind it.
claims.text: The blood long form (C1) is Hebrew in origin.
claims.verdict_note: The Hebrew-origin claim, under the spec §2 definition's second clause: unattested despite a checkable record that should contain it; additionally traceable to a 1994 theological discussion that produces no Hebrew proverb.

claims.layer_a: None for the curiosity saying either; its documented record runs through the London stage (Jonson; Shakespeare's company) and English/Irish print.
claims.layer_b: For curiosity, no Hebrew source is suggested by Phrase Finder, Brewer, Mair, or any corpus citation consulted.
claims.layer_c: The same step added, for this saying.
claims.text: The curiosity long form (C2) is Hebrew in origin.
claims.verdict_note: The Hebrew-origin claim for this saying, unattested despite a checkable record that should contain it.

claims.layer_a: None for the Jack saying either; its documented record runs through an English prison tract with a Latin analogue.
claims.layer_b: For Jack, no Hebrew source is suggested anywhere consulted; the framing for C5/C6 appears to be the generic 'ancient wisdom reversed' template applied beyond its C4 seed.
claims.layer_c: The same step added, for this saying.
claims.text: The Jack long form (C3) is Hebrew in origin.
claims.verdict_note: The Hebrew-origin claim for this saying, unattested despite a checkable record that should contain it.

entries.entry_verdict_line: Of the three 'ancient originals,' one comeback line is genuinely a century old — and none of the three is ancient, Hebrew, or an original.
open_questions: The Jack tail's exact first appearance beyond 'circulating online by at least 2005' (a non-specialist tracing; the load-bearing fact is the absence of any pre-internet attestation).
Whether the c.1180 German line is the same proverb (sources disagree).
1909 vs 1912 as the rejoinder's first print (both reported; the conclusion stands either way).
'Master of none' has no single agreed first date (1721 for the idea in variant wording vs 1785 for the exact modern wording — both recorded in the layers, neither chosen).
The viral video itself was not identified for this study.

Confidence, recorded here because the format carries no separate confidence field: the research rates the blood and curiosity findings high, the Jack tail's modernity high, and its exact 2005/2006 dating medium.
sources: Wikipedia entries citing the Oxford Dictionary of Proverbs (Speake & Simpson 2008) and the dated newspaper record
Phrase Finder / Gary Martin on all three sayings
BookBrowse, Proverbicals, Idioms Online, Omniglot on Jack
The Epoch Times-republished tracing of the tail (2005/2006)

teaching_notes.a: Safe as fact: the Layer A record with its hedges attached — a date or form taught from this entry is taught with its recorded uncertainty: the 1994 first appearance of the covenant/womb wording, the rejoinder's documented early-1900s arrival and standard use since, the staged accretion of 'master of none,' the absence of any Hebrew attestation, the short proverb's documented family-first meaning. The items in open questions (the c.1180 line's identity as the same proverb; 1909-vs-1912; the 'master of none' first date) are taught as open, never as settled.
teaching_notes.b: As 'some claim' (Donnie's own preparation only; never part of the teaching layer's read): the covenant/womb 'original,' the Hebrew-origin framing, the 'better than a master of one' ending — attributed to their modern sources (1994; 2000s popular-etymology; internet circulation), never stated as recovered antiquity.
teaching_notes.c: The lesson the true history carries: a sentence invented in 1994 can be believed by millions to be 3,000 years old within one generation — which is why a word's authority is its attestations, and why this shelf checks before it teaches.

entries.title: The claim that 'blood is thicker than water,' 'curiosity killed the cat,' and 'Jack of all trades, master of none' are cut-down versions of longer Hebrew originals whose meanings were reversed — checked against the print record.
